title: Deep in one: Genesis
for: I want to know Genesis well
subtitle: Twelve sessions through the book of beginnings, section by section: creation, the fall, the flood, Abraham, Jacob and Joseph, read with the Study Bible's notes.
intro: This track reads Genesis whole, a section at a sitting. The book has two halves. Chapters 1 to 11 tell the story of the whole world, from creation to the scattering at Babel. Chapters 12 to 50 narrow to one family, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, chosen for the sake of all the families of the earth. A heading runs through both halves, ‘This is the account of’, and it marks the book's sections the way chapter breaks mark ours.

Each session opens a chapter of the Study Bible with its notes in plain words, and comes back to one question, one thing to do and one verse. Read the whole section the session names before you begin it. Genesis is honest about its people, and some of its chapters are hard: a flood, a son on an altar, a sister wronged, a brother sold. The track doesn't hurry past them. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Deep in one: Genesis. The group meets twelve times and reads a section of the book each time, from the first chapter to the last. It suits people who already believe and people who are only curious, because Genesis raises the questions everyone asks: where the world came from, what went wrong with us, and whether God keeps his word to people who don't deserve it.

Each person reads the chapters and the session before the group meets. The meeting reads the heart of the section aloud and talks it over, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, small enough that everyone speaks. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for twelve meetings, and keep the end time you promised. Some sessions cover several chapters, so ask people to read ahead, and don't try to discuss every scene in the room. A leader doesn't need to be a scholar. A leader needs to have read the chapters and their notes, and to be willing to admit not knowing.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit in a circle round a table if you can, with the text open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone. Genesis is a story, and stories are best heard, so ask a good reader to read the central scene aloud at each meeting, and let people take turns. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about their own lives stays in the room, and that no one has to pray aloud.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Fifteen minutes: one person reads the central scene of the section aloud while the others follow.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is in the text.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse to keep, and the group says what it noticed in it.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words.
Five minutes: name the next section and the page its session opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Genesis raises some of the Bible's most argued questions: the days of creation and the age of the earth, the sons of God in chapter 6, a flood that covers the world, God telling Abraham to offer his son. When the group reaches one, read the note on it together before anyone answers. Where faithful Christians read a passage in more than one way, give each reading its strongest form and don't settle for the group what the church has not settled. If no one knows, write the question down and bring it back the next week.

Some questions are about whether any of it is true, or about how the church has used these chapters. Welcome them. A story like the curse on Canaan was once misused to defend slavery, and the notes name that misuse and reject it. The Honest Answers and the case for the faith take up many of these questions, and the sessions link several. Treating a question as disloyalty ends the conversation, and Genesis itself is full of people arguing with God.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Genesis is a family story, and families in it do real harm: a brother killed, a slave woman sent into the desert, daughters offered to a mob, a son sold by his brothers, a father who loves one child more than the rest. Their stories will touch someone's own. When that happens, stop the discussion and listen. Thank the person for saying it, don't explain their suffering for them, and don't hurry them back to the passage. Ask whether they would like the group to go on or to pause, and speak with them on their own afterwards.

Never let a line from Genesis be turned into a reason for someone to stay where they are being harmed, or into a quick comfort for fresh grief. Joseph's words about evil meant for good were said many years later, by the one who was wronged. If someone says that a partner, a parent, a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, fear or guilt that will not let them rest, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: In the beginning
teaching: Genesis opens with a sentence that settles more than it explains: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). Before you ask how long it took, ask what kind of writing this is. Chapter 1 is patterned like no ordinary story. God speaks, it is so, God sees that it is good, and there is evening and morning. The first three days give the world its shape, and the next three fill what was shaped. Its first hearers lived beside peoples whose creation stories began with a war among gods. Genesis has no war. The sun and moon aren't gods at all. They are lamps, set in the sky by the one God who has no rival.

Christians who hold Scripture as God's word read the days in more than one way. Some read them as ordinary days and the earth as young. Some read each day as a long age, some see a literary frame, some a week in which God sets up the world as his temple, and some hold that God made living things through the long process biology describes. Augustine, centuries before modern geology, argued that God made all things at once and that the six days were not days as we count them. This track leaves that question open, as the notes do. It doesn't leave open what the chapter confesses: one God made everything, made it good, and made man and woman alike in his image.

open.label: Genesis 1, passage by passage
open.why: Each passage of the first chapter in plain words, with what its first hearers would have heard and the readings Christians hold on the days.

also.label: How should a Christian read Genesis 1?
also.why: The main readings of the days, each in the form its own defenders would sign, and what every one of them shares.

also.label: Was Genesis 1 answering Babylon, not modern science?
also.why: The creation stories of Israel's neighbours set beside Genesis, and what the contrast shows about the God it confesses.

also.label: Creation and the image of God
also.why: Seven short pictures of creation out of nothing, a world called very good, and what it means for every person to bear God's image.

sessions.question: Genesis 1 tells you that every person you meet bears the image of God. Who in your week is hardest for you to see that way?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 1 aloud and mark every phrase that repeats. Then read Genesis 2 and write down two things it tells you about people that chapter 1 does not.

verse.text: So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.

group.open: What were you first told about Genesis 1, at school, at church or at home?
discuss: Genesis 1 has no war among gods and makes the sun a lamp. What would that have said to people who worshipped the sun?
Christians read the days in several ways. What does it do to a group when that question is held open rather than settled?
Chapter 2 tells the story again from the ground, with dust and breath and a garden. What does it add about what a human being is?
group.pray: Give thanks in your own words for the world and the people in it, each one made in God's image, and name before God one person you find hard to see that way.

sessions.title: The fall
teaching: Genesis 3 doesn't explain where evil came from. It shows how it gets into a life. The serpent starts with a question that makes God sound stingy, and the woman and the man take what they were told not to take. Their eyes are opened, and the first thing they see is themselves. They sew leaves, and when they hear God in the garden they hide. The first thing God says to the man afterwards is a question, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). God knew the answer. He asked so that the man would come out and say it.

What follows is judgment: pain in childbirth, a ground that fights the farmer, a bond between man and woman bent toward rule, and the way back to the tree of life closed. Yet inside the words to the serpent there is a promise that the woman's offspring will crush its head (3:15). Christians since Irenaeus in the second century have read that line as the first announcement of the gospel, and the notes set that reading beside the plainer one. Before the couple leave the garden, God makes garments of skin and clothes them himself. Judgment and mercy arrive in the same chapter, and they have never been far apart since.

open.label: Genesis 3, passage by passage
open.why: The serpent's question, the hiding, the judgments and the promise of 3:15, each explained in plain words with the hard questions they raise.

also.label: The fall, in the Bible's story
also.why: Where Genesis 3 stands in the whole story of the Bible, and how the rest of Scripture answers what went wrong in the garden.

also.label: Sin, in the Study Bible
also.why: What the whole Bible says sin is, how it spread from the garden, and what the church has confessed about it.

sessions.question: Where do you recognise in yourself the instinct to hide, from God or from the people closest to you?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 3 and list every question asked in the chapter and who asks it. Then read the note on 3:15 and its two readings, and write down which one you find more persuasive and why.

verse.text: But the LORD God called out to the man, “Where are you?”

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When you were a child, what did you do when you knew you had done something wrong?
discuss: The serpent never tells an outright lie at first. It asks a question. Why is a question about God's goodness so effective?
The man blames the woman and the woman blames the serpent. Where do you see that pattern of blame today, in families or in public life?
God clothes the couple before they leave the garden. What does that small act say about how God judges?
group.pray: Bring to God in silence one place where each of you has been hiding, and give thanks that he still comes into the garden asking where we are.

sessions.title: Cain, the flood, and a rainbow
teaching: Within a generation of the garden, the wrong done against God becomes a brother's blood. God warns Cain that “sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it” (Genesis 4:7), and Cain kills Abel in a field anyway. Then comes a genealogy with a refrain, a long life and then the end of it, broken once by Enoch, who walked with God. By chapter 6 the whole earth is full of violence, and the chapter says something startling about God: that he was grieved in his heart. The flood is told as creation run backwards, the waters above and below returning to cover what God had separated.

The surprise comes after the water goes down. God looks at the same human heart, evil from its youth, and this time it is the reason for patience, not judgment. He makes a covenant with Noah and every living creature and sets his bow in the clouds. Then the rescued family fails at once: Noah drunk, a son who shames him, a curse on Canaan. That curse was once twisted into the curse of Ham and used to defend the enslaving of Africans. The notes name that misuse and reject it, and so should every reader.

open.label: Genesis 6, passage by passage
open.why: The sons of God, a grieved God and the building of the ark, explained in plain words, with the old readings of the hardest verses set out fairly.

also.label: Hard passages
also.why: Every hard passage the notes take up, book by book. In Genesis, look for Cain's wife, the sons of God, a God who regrets, and the curse on Canaan.

also.label: Reading the genealogies
also.why: Why the Bible stops a story for a list of names, and how to read Genesis 5 and 11 without skipping them.

sessions.question: God's verdict on the human heart is the same before the flood and after it. Why do you think the second time it leads to a promise?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 4 and Genesis 9 side by side. Write down one sentence from each chapter that tells you how God treats people who have done wrong.

verse.text: I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth.

care: If this story frightens you, remember how it ends: God promises never to do it again (9:11). If you have lived through a flood or a storm, it was not a sign that God had shut a door on you. Talk to someone you trust about what you carry, and the Find Help page has people you can call.

group.open: Is there a story in your family about brothers or sisters who fell out and never made it up?
discuss: God speaks to Cain before he acts and warns him. What does that say about the choices in front of us?
Genesis says God was grieved in his heart before the flood. How does that change the way you picture the flood?
The family rescued from the flood fails almost at once. Why do you think Genesis tells us that?
group.pray: Pray for anyone you know caught in a family quarrel that has gone on for years, and give thanks for a God who binds himself by promise to a world that keeps failing him.

sessions.title: Babel and the call of Abram
teaching: The first half of Genesis ends with a city. The people of Babel say, “let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens, that we may make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). God scatters them, and the story narrows through a list of names to one man and his wife, and to a sentence that sounds like the end of a line: “But Sarai was barren; she had no children” (Genesis 11:30). Then God speaks to Abram, and the first thing he promises is the thing Babel tried to grab. Babel wanted to make a name. God promises to make Abram's name great.

The promise has three strands that run through the rest of the Bible: a land, a people descended from a childless couple, and blessing for all the families of the earth through them. Paul calls that last promise the gospel announced to Abraham in advance (Galatians 3:8). God chooses one family for the sake of everyone else. And the man of promise goes straight down to Egypt and passes his wife off as his sister to save his own skin. Genesis doesn't hide its heroes' failures. It wants you to see that the promise rests on God, not on the people who carry it.

open.label: Genesis 12, passage by passage
open.why: The call of Abram, the three promises and the trouble in Egypt, each explained in plain words, with what its first hearers would have noticed.

also.label: Abraham's road
also.why: A moving map of the places Genesis names, in the order it tells them, from Ur and Haran down into Canaan and Egypt and back.

also.label: Abraham, in the Bible's story
also.why: Where the call of Abraham stands in the whole story, and how the promise to bless every family of the earth is kept.

also.label: Genesis in the Study Bible
also.why: Who wrote Genesis and when, how its ten headings divide the book, and how its two halves fit together.

sessions.question: Babel tried to make a name for itself and Abram was given one. Where are you trying to make a name for yourself?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 11 and 12 together, from the tower to Egypt. Then trace Abram's road on the map, and note how far a man in his seventies was asked to go.

verse.text: I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.

group.open: Have you ever moved somewhere without knowing what you would find? What was it like?
discuss: Genesis moves from the whole world to one family. Why would God choose one family for the sake of every other?
Abram obeys at once in chapter 12 and lies in Egypt a few verses later. What does it do to you that the Bible tells both?
The promise is that all the families of the earth will be blessed. How should that shape the way a church sees people outside it?
group.pray: Give thanks that God's promise rests on him and not on us, and pray for one family each of you knows that needs to see God's kindness this week.

sessions.title: Covenant under the stars
teaching: Years pass and there is still no son. In chapter 15 Abram says so to God plainly, and God takes him outside to count the stars. Then comes one of the most important sentences in the Bible: “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). Paul builds his argument in Romans 4 on it, and so do the reformers after him. Abram had done nothing yet but listen to a promise and trust the one who made it, and God counted that trust as righteousness.

Then God seals the promise in a way its first hearers would have understood at once. Animals are cut in two, and when it is dark a smoking firepot and a flaming torch pass between the halves. In the ancient world a man who walked between the pieces called down on himself the fate of the animals if he broke his word. Jeremiah describes the same rite (Jeremiah 34:18). Here only God passes through, while Abram sleeps. In chapter 17 God renames Abram as Abraham, father of many nations, and gives circumcision as the sign of the covenant on the body of every male in the household.

open.label: Genesis 15, passage by passage
open.why: The stars, the faith credited as righteousness and the strange ceremony of the cut animals, each explained in plain words.

also.label: What is a biblical covenant?
also.why: The ancient treaty form behind God's covenants, and what it meant for a king to bind himself by oath to a weaker party.

also.label: Promises that build: the covenants
also.why: Seven pictures of the covenants laid one on another like the stones of an arch, from Noah's rainbow to the cup Jesus shared.

also.label: Justification, in the Study Bible
also.why: How the whole Bible speaks of being counted righteous before God, and where Christians agree and differ about it.

sessions.question: Abram was counted righteous for trusting a promise he could not yet see kept. What promise of God do you find hardest to trust?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 15 and 17, then Romans 4. Write down in two sentences why Paul thinks it matters that Abraham believed before he was circumcised.

verse.text: Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.

group.open: What is the most serious promise anyone has ever made to you?
discuss: In chapter 15 Abram complains to God openly, and God answers him. What does that say about honest prayer?
Only God passes between the pieces while Abram sleeps. What does that picture say about who keeps this covenant?
Paul reads Genesis 15:6 as the heart of the gospel. How would you put what it means in your own words?
group.pray: Name before God a promise of his that each of you finds hard to trust, and give thanks that he bound himself to keep his word.

sessions.title: Hagar, Ishmael and Sodom
teaching: Chapter 16 shows what happens when people try to help God keep his promise. Sarai gives Hagar, her Egyptian slave, to Abram, and when Hagar conceives the household turns cruel. Hagar runs into the desert, and the angel of the LORD finds her by a spring. She is a foreign slave woman, used and discarded, and she gives the LORD a name of her own: “You are the God who sees me” (Genesis 16:13). Years later, in chapter 21, she and her son Ishmael are sent away, and God hears the boy crying under a bush and opens her eyes to a well.

In chapter 18 Abraham welcomes three strangers with lavish hospitality, and Sarah laughs at the promise of a son. Then God tells Abraham what he means to do to Sodom, and Abraham argues with him, asking, “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25). Chapter 19 answers his hospitality with its opposite: a whole city surrounds Lot's house to violate his guests, and Lot offers his daughters to the mob. Genesis does not commend him. Ezekiel later names Sodom's sins as pride, plenty and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49).

open.label: Genesis 16, passage by passage
open.why: Sarai's plan, Hagar's flight and the God who sees, explained in plain words, with the hardest line in the chapter faced honestly.

also.label: Genesis 19, passage by passage
also.why: The angels in Sodom, Lot's offer and the fire from heaven, with what the rest of the Bible says Sodom's sin was.

also.label: What did hospitality mean in the ancient world?
also.why: Why a guest under your roof was sacred in the ancient Near East, and why Abraham's welcome and Sodom's assault are told side by side.

sessions.question: Hagar was seen by God when no one else in the household saw her. Who in your world is going unseen?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 16 and 21:8-21 as one story, Hagar's story. Write down everything God says and does for her, and what that tells you about who he notices.

verse.text: So Hagar gave this name to the LORD who had spoken to her: “You are the God who sees me,” for she said, “Here I have seen the One who sees me!”

care: A word for anyone who has been sent away by a parent, or a parent who has had to let a child go. Being sent away is not the end of being seen. God heard Ishmael under that bush. If you are carrying this, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you have nowhere safe to stay, the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

A word for anyone who has suffered sexual abuse within a family. This story does not call it right, and neither does the rest of the Bible. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If it is happening now, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever been welcomed into a home in a way you still remember?
discuss: Sarai's plan was legal and common in her world. What does Genesis want us to see in how it turned out?
Abraham argues with God about Sodom and God listens. What does that tell you about what prayer can be?
Abraham's welcome and Sodom's assault are told back to back. What does the contrast teach about how strangers should be treated?
group.pray: Pray for people who are going unseen where each of you lives, and give thanks that God is the one who sees.

sessions.title: The binding of Isaac
teaching: Chapter 22 begins by telling the reader what Abraham doesn't know: “God tested Abraham” (Genesis 22:1). Then God asks for the son of the promise, the one he waited twenty-five years for, and Abraham rises early and goes. Jewish readers call this story the Akedah, the binding. It is told with almost no feeling on the surface, and that is what makes it unbearable. Isaac carries the wood. He asks where the lamb is. His father answers, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son” (Genesis 22:8), and they walk on together.

It has never been an easy story, and it shouldn't be made easy. Some of Israel's neighbours offered children to their gods, and Israel's law would forbid it (Leviticus 18:21), and this story ends with a child spared and a ram in his place. Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead (Hebrews 11:19). Later Scripture places the temple on Mount Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1), and Christians have long seen in a beloved son carrying wood up a hill the shape of another Son. Read the notes slowly, and let the hard questions stand.

open.label: Genesis 22, the guided study
open.why: Seven steps through the chapter at your own pace, from reading it slowly to the questions it raises and what to carry from it.

also.label: Genesis 22, passage by passage
also.why: The test, the walk up the mountain and the ram in the thicket, with the hard questions faced honestly in plain words.

also.label: Faith, in the Study Bible
also.why: What the whole Bible means by faith, from Abraham's trust to the faith Hebrews 11 celebrates, and how it differs from certainty.

sessions.question: What do you find hardest in this chapter, and what would you want to ask Abraham on the way down the mountain?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 22 once without stopping, then read Hebrews 11:17-19. Write down what Hebrews says Abraham believed, and whether it changes how you read the chapter.

verse.text: Abraham answered, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.” And the two walked on together.

care: One thing must be said without any doubt. No one today is told by God to harm a child, or anyone else. This story has never been read in Jewish or Christian teaching as permission to hurt a child. If you hear a voice, or have a thought, telling you to harm a child or anyone else, do not act on it. Seek help at once: tell someone you trust, a doctor, or a pastor, today. If anyone is in immediate danger, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Is there a part of the Bible you have always found hard to read? Which one?
discuss: The reader is told it is a test and Abraham is not. How does knowing that change the way you read the chapter?
Isaac carries the wood and asks where the lamb is. Why do you think Christians have read this story alongside the cross?
The chapter ends with a ram caught in a thicket. What does the place name, The LORD Will Provide, mean to you?
group.pray: Bring to God the questions this chapter leaves with each of you, and give thanks for the Son who was not spared, offered for us.

sessions.title: Jacob's deceit, and the ladder
teaching: Jacob is born holding his brother's heel, and his name sounds like the Hebrew for heel, a word for someone who trips you from behind. He buys Esau's birthright for a bowl of stew, and in chapter 27, with his mother's plan and goat skins on his arms, he lies to his blind father to steal the blessing. The narrator doesn't stop to condemn anyone. Genesis trusts you to see it, and it lets the family pay. Esau plans to kill his brother, Jacob runs for his life, and the story never shows Rebekah seeing her favourite son again.

Then, alone in the open with a stone for a pillow, the cheat dreams of a stairway between earth and heaven, and God speaks. He doesn't rebuke Jacob. He gives him the promise made to Abraham and Isaac, and adds, “I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you” (Genesis 28:15). Jacob wakes and says the LORD was in this place and he didn't know it. Jesus takes up this dream when he tells Nathanael he will see angels going up and down on the Son of Man (John 1:51).

open.label: Genesis 27, passage by passage
open.why: The stolen blessing scene by scene, explained in plain words, with what a father's blessing meant in Jacob's world.

also.label: Genesis 28, passage by passage
also.why: Jacob's flight, the stairway at Bethel and the promise renewed, with the later passages that take the dream up.

also.label: Reading biblical narrative
also.why: How the Bible's stories teach without stopping to comment, and how to notice what the narrator leaves for you to judge.

sessions.question: God met Jacob on the night he was running from what he had done. What would it mean for God to meet you at your worst rather than your best?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 27 and 28. Mark every deception in chapter 27 and who it hurts. Then read 28:10-22 and write down what God promises and what he doesn't mention.

verse.text: When Jacob woke up, he thought, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.”

group.open: Did anyone in your family have a favourite? How did it shape the rest of you?
discuss: Isaac, Rebekah, Esau and Jacob all play a part in chapter 27. Who do you think is most to blame, and why?
Genesis tells this story without a word of judgment from the narrator. What does it trust its readers to do?
God gives Jacob the promise without a rebuke. Is that grace, or does it let him off? How would you answer?
group.pray: Pray for families where favouritism has done harm, your own included, and give thanks that God meets people in the place they are running from.

sessions.title: Jacob wrestles
teaching: Twenty years later Jacob is coming home, with wives, children and flocks, and Esau is coming to meet him with four hundred men. For the first time Jacob prays like a man who knows what he is, saying he is unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness God has shown him (Genesis 32:10). He sends gifts ahead in waves, sends his family across the river, and is left alone at the ford of the Jabbok. There a man wrestles with him until daybreak.

Jacob won't let go until he is blessed, and the stranger asks him his name. It is the hardest question in the story, because his name is the heel-grabber, and to say it is to confess what he has been. He says it. And he is given a new one: Israel, because he has struggled with God and with men and prevailed. He limps away into the sunrise, and the nation that takes his name is named after a man who wrestled God and came away wounded and blessed. Hosea remembers it centuries later: Jacob wept and sought his favour.

open.label: Genesis 32, passage by passage
open.why: Jacob's prayer, the gifts sent ahead and the night at the Jabbok, explained in plain words, with the readings of who the man was.

also.label: Is it okay to be angry at God?
also.why: Jacob, Job and the psalmists all struggled with God openly. Why Scripture keeps those prayers, and what they are not.

also.label: Prayer, in the Study Bible
also.why: What the whole Bible teaches about prayer, from Jacob's struggle at the river to the prayer Jesus taught.

sessions.question: Jacob had to say his own name before he received a new one. What would you have to admit about yourself before God?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 32 and 33. Write down Jacob's prayer in 32:9-12 in your own words, then note how Esau actually meets him in chapter 33.

verse.text: Then the man said, “Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed.”

group.open: Is there a meeting you have dreaded for years? What happened, or what do you imagine would happen?
discuss: Jacob prays humbly and still sends gifts to buy Esau off. What does that mix of faith and scheming look like in us?
The stranger asks Jacob his name. Why might saying it be the turning point of the night?
Jacob leaves blessed and limping. Why do you think the blessing came with a wound?
group.pray: Bring to God in silence the struggles each of you is carrying with him, and ask for the courage to hold on until he blesses.

sessions.title: Joseph sold, and in Egypt
teaching: Jacob, who was his mother's favourite, makes Joseph his own favourite and gives him a robe of many colours, and his brothers can't speak a kind word to him. Joseph tells them his dreams, which doesn't help. They throw him in a pit, sell him to traders for twenty pieces of silver, and dip the robe in a goat's blood to show their father. Jacob once deceived his own father with a goat's skins. Now his sons deceive him with a goat's blood. Genesis lets the echo speak for itself.

In Egypt Joseph is a slave, then falsely accused by his master's wife, then a prisoner forgotten by the man he helped for two full years. Through all of it one line keeps returning: the LORD was with Joseph (Genesis 39:2, 21, 23). It is said of him in a slave's quarters and in a prison, which is exactly where most people would say God had left. When Pharaoh calls him at last, Joseph refuses the credit for what he is about to do: God, he says, will give Pharaoh his answer.

open.label: Genesis 37, passage by passage
open.why: The robe, the dreams, the pit and the sale into Egypt, explained in plain words, with a family's harm faced honestly.

also.label: Genesis 39, passage by passage
also.why: Joseph in Potiphar's house and in prison, and the line that keeps returning, that the LORD was with him.

also.label: Providence, in the Study Bible
also.why: What Scripture teaches about God's rule over ordinary and terrible events, and the questions Christians still wrestle with.

also.label: The Bible's timeline
also.why: Where the patriarchs and Joseph's years in Egypt fall in the Bible's long story, set out from the book pages' own words.

sessions.question: Genesis says the LORD was with Joseph in a prison. Where have you been tempted to decide God was absent?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 37 and 39 to 41. Mark each time the text says the LORD was with Joseph, and note where Joseph was each time.

verse.text: And the LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, serving in the household of his Egyptian master.

care: A word for anyone who has been sold, traded, or forced to work or to do sexual acts by someone who controls them, or who is in that place now. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is something you were sure of at seventeen that you see differently now?
discuss: Jacob's favouritism and Joseph's dreams both feed the brothers' hatred. Is anyone in this family without fault?
The goat's blood echoes Jacob's own deception of his father. What does Genesis want us to see in that echo?
Joseph is forgotten in prison for two full years. How do you hold on to God in a wait that long?
group.pray: Pray for people who are in a pit or a prison of any kind tonight, and for anyone in the group who feels forgotten.

sessions.title: Joseph and his brothers
teaching: Famine drives Joseph's brothers to Egypt, and they bow before a governor they don't recognise. Joseph tests them for a long time, and the test is whether they will do to Benjamin, the new favourite, what they once did to him. The turning point is Judah, the brother who first proposed selling Joseph. He offers to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place, so that the boy can go home to his father (Genesis 44:33). The man who sold one brother now gives himself for another.

Then Joseph can't hold back. He sends everyone out and weeps so loudly the Egyptians hear it, and he tells them he is Joseph, their brother, “the one you sold into Egypt” (Genesis 45:4). Forgiveness here doesn't pretend nothing happened. It names the wrong in full and then refuses to let it have the last word, because God sent him ahead to save lives. Joseph is not quick or soft. He forgives as someone who has tested whether his brothers have changed.

open.label: Genesis 45, passage by passage
open.why: Joseph makes himself known, weeps over his brothers and sends for his father, explained in plain words with care for those still being hurt.

also.label: Genesis 44, passage by passage
also.why: The silver cup in Benjamin's sack and Judah's long speech offering himself in the boy's place, explained in plain words.

also.label: How to forgive someone who has not apologized
also.why: What forgiveness is and is not, why it does not require pretending, and how it differs from trust and reconciliation.

sessions.question: Joseph named the wrong before he forgave it. Is there a wrong done to you that you have not yet been able to name honestly?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 42 to 45 in one sitting. Then read Judah's speech in 44:18-34 aloud, and write down what has changed in him since chapter 37.

verse.text: Then Joseph said to his brothers, “Please come near me.” And they did so. “I am Joseph, your brother,” he said, “the one you sold into Egypt! And now, do not be distressed or angry with yourselves that you sold me into this place, because it was to save lives that God sent me before you.”

care: If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever been reunited with someone after a long silence? What was the first thing said?
discuss: Joseph tests his brothers before he reveals himself. Was that wisdom, or something less kind? What makes you think so?
Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place. Where else in the Bible does someone take another's place?
Joseph names what was done to him and forgives it. How is that different from saying it doesn't matter?
group.pray: Bring to God, each in silence, a person you have not been able to forgive, and ask for honesty about the wrong and the grace not to let it have the last word.

sessions.title: You meant it for evil
teaching: Jacob dies in Egypt and is carried home to be buried, and the brothers are terrified that Joseph has only been waiting for their father to go. They send a message asking forgiveness, and Joseph weeps. Then he says the line the whole book has been moving toward: “Am I in the place of God? As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this” (Genesis 50:19-20). He doesn't say the evil was good. He says God was at work beneath it.

That sentence was said by the one who was wronged, many years later, looking back. It was never said to him in the pit, and it isn't a line to hand to someone in fresh pain. Genesis began in a garden with God giving life. It ends with a coffin in Egypt, far from the land of promise. But Joseph made his brothers swear to carry his bones home when God came for them, and the book closes on a body waiting for a promise. Carry that into your week. The next track in this program takes you into the Psalms, the prayers of people still waiting.

open.label: Genesis 50, passage by passage
open.why: Jacob's burial, the brothers' fear, Joseph's answer and his bones, explained in plain words, with care for anyone reading in grief.

also.label: Genesis: the book of beginnings
also.why: The whole book in seven pictures, its two halves and its ten headings, to look back on what you have read from the garden to the coffin.

also.label: If God is good, why is there suffering?
also.why: The hardest question Joseph's story raises, taken at its strongest, and what the Christian faith does and does not claim in answer.

also.label: Deep in one: the Psalms
also.why: The next track in this program, Deep in one: the Psalms, gives ten sessions to praying the prayers Jesus prayed.

sessions.question: Joseph could say God meant it for good only years later. What in your life are you still too close to see?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 50, then go back and read Genesis 1. Write down one way the last chapter answers the first, and one thing it leaves still waiting.

verse.text: As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people.

care: A word of care. Some readers come to this chapter grieving a father or a mother. Joseph's tears were not a lack of faith, and yours are not either. If your grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a grief counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

It is said by the one who was wronged, looking back many years later, when he could see what came of it. It is not something others said to him while he was in the pit, or in chains, or in prison. So it is never a line to hand to someone in fresh grief. And it is never a reason to explain away abuse, or to tell someone who has been hurt that the harm was really good for them. If someone has hurt you, what they did was wrong. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Which of these twelve sessions will you remember longest, and why?
discuss: Joseph says God meant it for good but never says the evil was good. Why does that distinction matter?
Genesis begins in a garden and ends with a coffin in Egypt. What is the book telling us is still unfinished?
Joseph's bones wait for a promise. What are you waiting on God for, and how will you wait?
group.pray: Give thanks by name for each person in the group, and ask that each would carry what they have seen in Genesis into the week ahead, still waiting on the God who keeps his word.
